extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theology and early-modern political philosophy (readers of Hobbes/Leviathan)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative claims about the relation of civil sovereignty and religion from an early-modern political-theological chapter (discussing Abraham, Moses, priests, kings, and Christ). Useful for analysis of sovereign authority over religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single chief governor to avoid religious faction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Governour both of the State, and of the Religion, forbiddeth to be taught: And that Governor must be one; or else there must needs follow Faction, and Civil war in the Common-wealth...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that having one chief pastor/sovereign for religion prevents conflicting doctrines, faction, and civil war — including internal division in individuals ('between the Christian, and the Man').

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive commands from sovereign when no immediate revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: “they to whom God hath not spoken immediately, are to receive the positive commandements of God, from their Soveraign; as the family and seed of Abraham did from Abraham...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where people lack direct supernatural revelation, they must accept the sovereign's articulation of divine commands for external acts and profession of religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between external religious acts and inward belief
rubrics_metrics.description: “As for the inward Thought, and beleef of men... they are not voluntary, nor the effect of the laws... and consequently fall not under obligation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws (and sovereign authority) can govern external behavior and profession but not the private inward faith or conscience, which belong to God alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign may punish private revelations opposing state religion
rubrics_metrics.description: “it was not unlawfull for Abraham... to punish them; and consequently that it is lawfull now for the Soveraign to punish any man that shall oppose his Private Spirit against the Laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private pretensions to visions or spirits that contradict the sovereign's religious rules may be punished to maintain public order and uniform doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign as sole interpreter of what God hath spoken for the commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: “none but the Soveraign in a Christian Common-wealth, can take notice what is, or what is not the Word of God... they that have the place of Abraham in a Common-wealth, are the onely Interpreters of what God hath spoken.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretive authority over Scripture and doctrine within a commonwealth rests with the person who represents God's person on earth (the sovereign).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of a leader depends on people's consent and belief in his mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: “His authority therefore... must be grounded on the Consent of the People, and their Promise to obey him... for 'the people'... 'when they saw the Thunderings... they said unto Moses, speak thou with us, and we will hear'.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even prophetic or mediatorial authority (as with Moses) is supported by the people's assent, often produced by signs, miracles, or the people's promise to obey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founder of polity has sovereign power while establishing order
rubrics_metrics.description: “whosoever ordereth, and establisheth the Policy, as first founder of a Common-wealth... must needs have Soveraign Power over the people all the while he is doing of it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The person who organizes and establishes the polity wields sovereign authority during that formative period (applied to Moses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on access to divine communication reserved to sovereign representative
rubrics_metrics.description: “No man upon pain of death might be so presumptuous as to approach the Mountain where God talked with Moses... To look upon them... is allowed; but to interpret them... is to transgresse the bounds God hath set us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The populace may hear/read Scripture but must not usurp the sovereign's prerogative to interpret divine communications; overstepping is framed as irreverent and unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophets and inspired ministers are authorized and subordinate to sovereign's spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: “there were... Seventy men, that are said to Prophecy... and these were of all Moses his election... God came down... and took of the Spirit that was upon Moses, and gave it to the Seventy Elders... endued them with a mind conformable, and subordinate to that of Moses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prophecy and inspired speech are permitted only when authorized and understood as subordinate extensions of the sovereign's mind/authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priesthood (High Priest) as viceregent with supreme authority under God
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Kingdome, as being a Sacerdotall Kingdome, descended... to Aarons Son, Eleazar the High Priest... the Supreme Power of making War and Peace, was in the Priest. The Supreme Power of Judicature belonged also to the High Priest...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the covenantal arrangement, the hereditary priest (High Priest) held combined civil and ecclesiastical supremacy — control over worship, war/peace, and adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary judges do not displace ordinary sovereign right
rubrics_metrics.description: “the Judges... were men chosen by God extraordinarily... were obeyed... not out of duty, but out of reverence... it cannot bee drawn into argument against the Right the High Priest had to the Soveraign Power.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary, extraordinary saviors/judges (like the judges in Israel) do not negate the permanent sovereign rights held by established religious or civil offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: When people demand a king they may displace priestly supremacy
rubrics_metrics.description: “they signified that they would no more bee governed by the commands that should bee laid upon them by the Priest... they deposed that peculiar Government of God... Having therefore rejected God... there was no authority left to the Priests, but such as the King was pleased to allow them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A collective popular decision to institute a monarchy transfers supreme civil and religious authority to the king, reducing priestly autonomy to what the king permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: King's supremacy includes religion as well as civil governance
rubrics_metrics.description: “for the Government of Civill affaires, it is manifest, it was all in the hands of the King... In which is contained also the ordering of Religion... the King had full Power, both Temporall and Spirituall.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The king exercises supremacy over both secular policy and external religion; religious ordering falls under royal prerogative when monarchy is accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice of rulers may differ from rightful supremacy; prophets can check kings
rubrics_metrics.description: “though the power both of State and Religion were in the Kings... none of them were uncontrolled in the use of it, but such as were gracious for their own naturall abilities... there were Prophets that alwaies controlled the Kings, for transgressing the Religion, and sometimes also for Errours of State.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice shows kings were subject to prophetic rebuke and constraints; de facto limitations exist even if the theoretical right is unity of sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-exilic disorder undermines settled claims about supremacy
rubrics_metrics.description: “During the Captivity, the Jews had no Common-wealth... after their return... there was no promise made of obedience... In such sort as nothing can be gathered from their confusion... concerning the Supremacy in either.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Periods without a settled commonwealth (exile, foreign rule) disrupt the clear assignment of civil/religious supremacy, making rights ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold office of Christ: Redeemer, Prophet/Pastor, King
rubrics_metrics.description: “We find in Holy Scripture three parts of the Office of the Messiah: the first of a Redeemer... The second of a Pastor, Counsellour, or Teacher... The third of a King, and Eternall King...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets out Christ's roles and maps them to corresponding times/actions (redemption by sacrifice, conversion by preaching/ministers, eternal reign at the Resurrection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ as Redeemer does not make him present earthly king before his death/resurrection
rubrics_metrics.description: “it is manifest, that our Saviour (as man) was not King of those that he Redeemed, before hee suffered death... he was not then King in present, by vertue of the Pact... which the faithfull make with him in Baptisme.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because redemption precedes possession, Christ's kingship over the redeemed is eschatological — fully realized only after his death and at the Resurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ's preaching did not intend to subvert existing civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: “he commanded to obey those that sate then in Moses chaire, and to pay tribute to Caesar... The Kingdome hee claimed was to bee in another world... how then could his words, or actions bee seditious, or tend to the overthrow of their then Civill Government?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Christ's ministry is framed as not contrary to Jewish civil law or Roman authority; teaching obedience to existing magistrates and refusing present judicial/political usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christ's final kingship subordinate to the Father and analogous to Moses's role
rubrics_metrics.description: “he is to be King then, no otherwise than as subordinate, or Viceregent of God the Father, as Moses was in the wildernesse... The Father... hath committed all judgment to the Son.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Christ exercises judgment/kingdom in the world to come, he does so under the Father's ultimate authority, mirroring the viceregal role of Moses and earlier priest-kings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sacraments and ministerial structures mirror earlier polity and authorize ministry
rubrics_metrics.description: “As Moses authorized Seventy Elders... so our Saviour also ordained seventy Disciples, to preach his Kingdome... our Saviour instituted [baptism] for a Sacrament to be taken by all that beleeved in him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institution of sacraments and delegation of ministers is presented as an orderly, authorized continuation of polity: sacraments admit into the kingdom; ministers are authorized agents of sovereign religious authority.
